intro: Most people in Borthwickside start thinking seriously about a wet room when an existing bathroom becomes difficult to use — whether that's for an ageing parent, a family member with reduced mobility, or simply because a cramped, dated shower enclosure has finally had enough. Wet rooms solve all of that in one go: a fully waterproofed, level-access space that's easier to clean, more practical to use, and genuinely adds value to a home. For a small village like Borthwickside, where properties tend to be well-loved and long-occupied, it's often a considered investment rather than an impulse decision — and that's exactly the right approach.
localContext: Borthwickside sits in Midlothian, and like much of the surrounding area, its housing stock is a real mix. You've got older stone-built properties and period cottages where bathroom floors might be uneven, walls are solid stone rather than stud partitions, and the pipework could be anything from decades-old lead to more recent copper. Then there are the modern estates where layout and access are more straightforward, but space can still be tight. Each property type comes with its own challenges for wet room installation. Stone walls need specialist waterproofing membranes and tanking systems that account for potential movement, while older floors may need levelling before any drainage can be properly set. Borthwickside is also in a moderately hard water area, which means limescale will build up on exposed fixtures over time — something worth factoring in when choosing taps, showerheads, and screen materials, as certain finishes hold up far better than others in these conditions.
serviceDetail: A professional wet room installation in Borthwickside typically follows a clear sequence, and understanding each stage helps you avoid surprises. It starts with a site survey, where the installer assesses your existing bathroom layout, checks floor joists or slab condition, and reviews drainage options. This step is especially important in older stone-built homes where the subfloor might not be what it appears. Once the plan is agreed, strip-out comes first — removing the existing suite, floor coverings, and any damaged plasterwork. The floor is then prepared and, if needed, built up using a specifically graded screed to create the correct fall toward the drain, usually around 1.5 to 2 degrees. Tanking follows — applying a waterproof membrane across every surface that could be exposed to moisture. This is not a step to cut corners on, particularly in Borthwickside's older properties where stone walls can be porous. After tanking is signed off, tiling or other wall finishes go on, along with the drain, thermostatic shower valve, and any additional fixtures. The final stage is sealing, testing, and a thorough clean-down. From start to finish, a standard installation in a single bathroom typically takes five to eight working days, depending on the complexity of the property.
pricing: In Borthwickside, a fully fitted wet room will generally cost between £6,500 and £12,000, with most projects landing in the £7,500 to £10,000 range. The main factors that push costs up are the age and condition of the existing bathroom, the complexity of the drainage layout, and whether significant structural work is needed — all things that come up more often in period cottages and older stone properties than in modern builds. Material choices matter too: high-end tiling, brassware, and thermostatic systems add up quickly. Budget separately for any decorating or plastering outside the immediate wet room area, as this is often not included in the installation quote.
whyLocal: For a project of this scale, using a tradesperson who knows Borthwickside and the surrounding Midlothian area properly makes a real difference. Local installers will have worked on similar stone-built properties before, they'll understand the quirks of older drainage systems, and they won't be guessing when it comes to building regs compliance in this part of Scotland. They're also easier to hold accountable if something needs attention after the job is done — a firm with a local reputation to protect tends to do neater work and communicate more honestly than someone who's driven up from elsewhere for the day.

faqs.q: Can a wet room be installed in an older stone-built cottage in Borthwickside?
faqs.a: Yes, but it requires more preparation than a modern property. Stone walls need thorough tanking, and floors often need levelling before the drain can be correctly positioned. An experienced installer will survey the space first and flag any structural issues. It's very achievable — just budget a little more time and cost compared to a new-build bathroom.

faqs.q: Will limescale be a problem with a wet room in Borthwickside's water supply?
faqs.a: Borthwickside has moderately hard water, so yes, limescale on showerheads and exposed fittings is a genuine consideration. Choosing chrome or brushed nickel finishes rather than matte black helps, and a decent thermostatic shower valve with an easy-clean nozzle makes maintenance much simpler. Some homeowners also install an inline scale reducer on the shower feed.

faqs.q: How long will a wet room installation take in Borthwickside?
faqs.a: For most homes in Borthwickside, allow five to eight working days for a full installation. Older properties sometimes take longer if the floor needs significant levelling or if unexpected issues come up during the strip-out — corroded pipework, for example, or a subfloor that needs reinforcing. Your installer should give you a realistic timeline after the initial survey.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission or building warrants for a wet room in Borthwickside?
faqs.a: In most cases, no planning permission is needed for a like-for-like bathroom conversion in Scotland. However, a building warrant may be required depending on the scope of structural work involved. Your installer should be familiar with Scottish building regulations and can advise you during the survey stage. Always confirm this in writing before work begins.
